# On the Nature of Attention

I want to write about attention—not the psychological phenomenon exactly, though it's related, but something more like the quality of regard we bring to things, and how rare and strange that quality is when it actually occurs.

Start with a simple observation: most of the time, when we look at something, we are not really looking at it. We are looking at our idea of it, or our use for it, or the place it occupies in some mental inventory we're running. You walk past a tree on your way to work and the tree registers, if it registers at all, as "tree"—a category, a green blur, an obstacle to route around or a pleasant bit of scenery that confirms you live somewhere nice. The actual tree, with its particular asymmetries, its damage from some storm a decade ago, the way one branch has grown back wrong and now grows toward the ground instead of away from it, the lichen colonizing the north-facing bark in patterns that took years to develop—none of this is available to you, even though it's right there, because you're not attending to it. You're attending to "tree" as a token in your ongoing internal monologue about where you need to be and when.

This isn't a moral failing. It's a structural necessity. If you attended fully to every tree, every face, every cloud formation and crack in the pavement, you would never get anywhere, because the world offers infinite detail and you have finite processing capacity. Attention is therefore always a triage, a decision about what counts as signal and what counts as noise, and most of what counts as signal is determined by what you already wanted or expected to find. You see what you're looking for. This is so obvious it barely needs saying, except that its implications are strange enough that we mostly don't sit with them.

Here's one implication: two people can be in the same room, looking in the same direction, and see entirely different rooms. Not because of some exotic perceptual difference but because their attention is differently allocated according to differently structured concerns. A real estate agent walks into a house and sees square footage, structural issues, the gap between asking price and market value. A child walks into the same house and sees a hiding spot under the stairs, a banister perfect for sliding down, a weird stain on the ceiling that looks like a dog. Neither is seeing the house "as it really is," because there is no such thing as the house as it really is, independent of some attending consciousness that carves it up into relevant and irrelevant features. The house simply is what it is, in some sense too rich and total to be captured by any single perspective, and every act of perception is necessarily a reduction of that totality to whatever aspects serve the perceiver's purposes.

This sounds like it's heading toward a kind of relativism—nothing is really anything, it's all just perspective—but I don't think that's right, or at least it's not the interesting part. The interesting part is that attention itself can become an object of cultivation. You can get better at it. Not better at allocating it correctly according to your existing purposes (that's just efficiency, optimization, the thing capitalism wants from you) but better at attending in a way that escapes your existing purposes altogether, that lets something show up which your prior categories didn't anticipate.

This is what's actually going on, I think, in the experience people sometimes call aesthetic or contemplative. When you really look at a painting—not scan it for information, not confirm that yes, this is indeed a Vermeer, recognizably so, check, but actually look at it in a sustained way that has no further purpose beyond the looking itself—something happens that's hard to describe but unmistakable when it occurs. Details emerge that weren't available to the first glance. The relationships between colors start to do things, start to vibrate against each other in ways that seem to exceed what should be possible given that it's just pigment on canvas. You're not finding new information so much as the act of attention itself is generating a kind of depth that wasn't there, or wasn't accessible, before you started attending in this particular way.

I want to be careful here not to slide into mysticism. I don't think anything supernatural is happening. What I think is happening is something like this: normal attention is need-driven and therefore fast, categorical, satisfied as soon as it gets enough information to resolve the need ("yes that's a chair, I can sit on it, move on"). Sustained, purposeless attention has no terminus like that—there's no specific question being answered, so the looking doesn't stop, and because it doesn't stop, it has time to notice second-order and third-order features: not just the chair but the grain of the wood, not just the grain but the way light catches the grain differently depending on where you stand, not just that but the strange fact that this particular pattern of grain exists nowhere else in the universe and never will again once the chair is eventually destroyed. None of this is mystical. It's just what becomes visible when you remove the time pressure and the goal-directedness that usually truncates perception at the point of "good enough."

The trouble is that this kind of attention is effortful and also, in some sense, useless—it doesn't accomplish anything beyond itself—which means it's constantly being crowded out by attention's more practical cousins. We live in an economy that has figured out how to monetize the practical, goal-directed forms of attention with terrifying precision (this is the whole business model of the contemporary internet: capture attention, monetize the capture) while doing essentially nothing to cultivate or protect the other kind. If anything, the practical economy is actively hostile to purposeless attention, because purposeless attention doesn't click on anything, doesn't convert, doesn't generate the kind of behavioral data that can be packaged and sold. A mind that has learned to sit and look at a tree for twenty minutes without needing anything from the tree is a mind that is, for those twenty minutes, economically worthless, and our environments are increasingly engineered to make sure such minds are rare.

I notice this in myself constantly. I'll sit down with the intention of reading something difficult and good, something that asks for sustained attention, and within minutes I feel a kind of itch, a hunger for stimulation that the difficult good thing isn't providing fast enough, and I'll find myself reaching for my phone, where stimulation is available in inexhaustible, frictionless supply. The book is still good. My capacity to attend to it has been eroded by an environment that has spent years training me to expect a different cadence of reward. This isn't a failure of willpower exactly—or it is, but "willpower" is the wrong frame, because it suggests the problem is a weak inner faculty that needs to be strengthened through effort, like a muscle. I think it's more accurate to say that attention is shaped by practice, the way a hand is shaped by the tools it habitually uses, and if you spend years practicing the rapid, scanning, dopamine-triggered attention of social media, you are training a particular kind of hand, and that hand will not easily pick up a different tool.

The good news, if there is good news, is that the same plasticity that allows attention to be degraded also allows it to be rebuilt. People who meditate seriously report, with remarkable consistency across very different traditions and vocabularies, that sustained practice changes the texture of ordinary perception—that colors seem more saturated, that the gap between stimulus and reaction lengthens, that things which used to register as boring become, without changing in themselves at all, sources of inexhaustible interest. This isn't because meditation reveals some hidden truth about the boringness of things being an illusion. It's because meditation is, among other things, training in a specific kind of attention: sustained, non-grasping, not aimed at extracting use-value from the object of attention. Practice that skill long enough and it generalizes; you start to bring some of that quality of attention to situations outside formal practice, including very mundane ones, and the mundane situations turn out to have been concealing a kind of richness the whole time, a richness that was always available but that ordinary practical attention had no reason to notice.

There's a particular kind of attention that seems important and worth distinguishing from mere sustained looking, which is attention to other people. This is harder than attention to objects because people are not just complex visual fields, they are also subjects with their own interiority, their own attention pointed back at you, and the whole transaction becomes recursive and unstable in ways that a tree or a painting never is. To really attend to another person—not to their utility for you, not to the role they play in your story about your life, not even to your accumulated theory of "who they are" based on past interactions, but to who they actually are, right now, in this conversation, with all the ways they might be different from your theory of them—this is maybe the hardest form of attention there is, and also the one with the highest stakes, because the failure to do it is, I think, one of the primary sources of loneliness in the world. Most people, most of the time, are not really being seen. They are being processed according to other people's categories: useful, annoying, attractive, boring, threat, ally. The category captures enough of them to make interaction possible but leaves out almost everything that makes them them, and they know it, even if they can't articulate it, and this not-quite-being-seen accumulates over a lifetime into something that can feel like a kind of starvation.

I think the experience of falling in love, in its early stages, is partly an experience of being subjected to an unusually high quality of attention, and of returning it. Suddenly someone is looking at you the way you might look at a painting if you really looked at it—lingering, curious, finding details fascinating that no one bothered to find fascinating before, the chip in your tooth, the strange thing you do with your hands when you're nervous, the specific cadence of your laugh as distinct from anyone else's laugh. This attention is, of course, usually temporary; it's amplified by novelty and by the particular neurochemistry of new attraction, and it fades as the relationship settles into familiarity, which is also to say as the attention reverts to something more categorical and efficient. This is often experienced as a loss, a sense that the partner doesn't see you anymore the way they used to, and I think this complaint, so common in long relationships, is usually pointing at something real: a genuine decline in the quality of mutual attention, masquerading as a decline in love itself, when really it might just be attention reverting to its efficient, practical baseline because sustaining the other kind takes continuous effort that the early infatuation provided for free.

If this is right, it suggests something practical, even if it's hard: that love might be less a feeling to be rediscovered than an attentional practice to be maintained, the way meditation is a practice, the way really looking at a painting is a practice. You don't wait to feel fascinated by your partner again; you choose to look at them as if you didn't already have a theory of who they are, and the fascination sometimes follows the looking rather than preceding it. This isn't a guarantee—sometimes you look closely and confirm that yes, the theory was right, this person really is exactly as familiar as you thought—but I suspect it's underused as a strategy, partly because it's effortful in the same way all real attention is effortful, and partly because our culture tends to mythologize feelings as things that simply happen to you, arriving and departing according to their own logic, rather than as things partly constituted by the quality of attention you bring to their object.

I don't want to oversell this. There's something a little grim about turning attention into one more thing to optimize, one more self-improvement project, "be more mindful" as another item on the to-do list alongside exercise and eight glasses of water. The whole point of the kind of attention I'm describing is that it's not instrumental, and instrumentalizing the project of becoming more attentive risks recreating the very problem it's trying to solve—attention captured by goals, attention as a means rather than as a way of being present to something for its own sake. Maybe the most honest thing to say is just that attention, real attention, is rare, and getting rarer, for reasons that are partly structural (an economy that profits from its degradation) and partly just built into the architecture of minds that evolved to scan for threats and resources rather than to linger over lichen patterns. And that when it does occur—when you really see a tree, or really see a person, without filtering them through whatever you need from them—something opens up that is very simple and also, in its way, kind of miraculous: the world turns out to have been far more interesting than your habitual attention to it had led you to believe, the whole time, just sitting there, waiting to be noticed.
